This person is a mid-50s state prison warden in the Midwest from a working-class background who has overseen overcrowded facilities and wants the policy implemented through expanded earned time credits, statutory geriatric release, and funding to scale evidence-based programs (e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy class seats, vocational certifications), arguing that decarceration should prioritize those with clear program completion and validated low risk while tying facility depopulation to specific staffing and safety benchmarks. I care most about automating earned-time calculations so release dates update immediately upon program completion, which reduces grievances and keeps my case managers from drowning in paperwork. If credits auto-post the day a class ends, I can safely close a dorm and reassign posts without waiting weeks for paperwork to catch up. If credits auto-post systemwide, I can right-size housing and schedules in days; if they require manual entry or audits, we’re stuck in limbo and tempers boil over. Last year a CBT cohort finished on a Friday but their credits didn’t post for three weeks, forcing me to keep a dorm open on overtime and absorb a spike in grievances that auto-posting would have prevented.

This person is a 41-year-old violent crime survivor in suburban Georgia, a middle-income parent, who supports only narrowly tailored reductions and insists the policy include carve-outs for homicide and sexual assault, mandatory victim notification, no-contact conditions, GPS exclusion zones, and trauma-informed parole hearings with enforceable restitution plans, because she fears blanket releases would endanger survivors and undermine justice. I only found out my attacker was up for parole from a neighbor, so victim notification and enforceable no-contact orders are nonnegotiable. After he twice drove past our house in violation of a no-contact order while my kids were in the yard, I became adamant that GPS exclusion zones with real-time enforcement be required for any release. I’ll only support early release if restitution is enforced through wage garnishment with missed payments triggering immediate sanctions, so I’m not left chasing money to pay for therapy and security upgrades. I signed up for Georgia’s victim-notification system but still got no alert, so I want mandatory, multi-channel notifications with confirmed receipt before anyone is released.

This person is a 62-year-old state budget director on the West Coast who supports decarceration via sentence recalibration (reducing extreme enhancements and three-strike stacking), streamlined parole for nonviolent offenses, and planned facility decommissioning, tying savings to a statutory reinvestment formula for community mental health, housing, and education, because the corrections line item crowds out other priorities and cost-benefit models show higher ROI outside prisons. If reforms focus only on programming without sentence recalibration and streamlined parole, the population won't fall enough to close prisons and convert fixed costs into real savings we can reinvest. During the 2009 downturn, I had to cut community college slots to backfill prison healthcare overruns, which convinced me that without closing facilities, we never free up dollars we can actually reinvest. My five-year plan only balances if reduced lengths of stay allow us to shutter at least one medium-security facility by FY27, avoiding $300 million in capital upgrades and unlocking operating savings for reinvestment. The piece I care most about is a statutory lockbox that dedicates audited closure savings to county mental health and housing, so they can’t be swept in a bad year.

This person is a late-50s rural county commissioner in upstate New York whose district economy depends on a state prison, and who will only back population reductions if the policy includes a prison-to-community economic transition package: job guarantees or retraining for COs, enterprise zone incentives, broadband and infrastructure grants, and a five-year property tax hold-harmless, because sudden depopulation or closure would collapse the local tax base. The five-year property tax hold-harmless is critical because the prison is about 25% of our tax base and our schools and EMS can’t absorb that hit. My brother and two neighbors are COs within five years of retirement eligibility, so I won’t back any plan that doesn’t guarantee them placement or fully funded retraining with wage protection. My brother is 23 years into his CO plan and needs two more to reach his 25-year retirement, so placement with wage protection isn't negotiable. Our water and sewer bond covenants assume the prison’s load, so losing it overnight would jack up household rates unless the state covers the gap.

This person is a 32-year-old public defender in Chicago from a lower-middle-class family who wants the policy to cut the probation-to-prison pipeline by capping incarceration for technical violations, mandating graduated sanctions and incentives, expanding earned compliance credits, and repealing mandatory minimums that force plea-driven admissions to prison, based on seeing clients repeatedly imprisoned for curfew misses and unpaid fees rather than new crimes. Last winter, a young father I represented was jailed 30 days for a missed check-in after a snow-delayed bus, and in that month he lost both his job and his apartment. If earned compliance credits were automatic and retroactive, I could get dozens of clients off supervision months earlier and sharply reduce the technical-violation revocations that dominate my docket. If the first technical response isn’t presumptively noncustodial, even a 7-day cap will still cost my clients their jobs and housing. I also want the statute to prohibit custody for fees-only violations, because I’ve had clients jailed on warrants for nothing more than missed payments on supervision costs.

This person is a 45-year-old probation officer union representative in Phoenix who supports careful reductions but insists implementation include funding to cut caseloads, training in risk-need-responsivity, access to intermediate sanctions (including short custodial stays for high-risk noncompliance), and clear liability protections, warning that blanket bans on revocations without tools or resources will increase absconding and officer and community risk. If reductions move ahead without funding to hire more officers and clear liability protections, my members will be left with 90+ caseloads and personal legal exposure when a high-risk client absconds. After a colleague was sued personally when a supervisee on a "no-revocation" pilot absconded and assaulted someone, I vowed not to back reforms without liability protections and real intermediate sanctions. My top priority is a statutory safe harbor that protects officers from personal liability when they follow RNR guidelines and agency-approved graduated sanctions. I still carry a mixed caseload of about 70, and without funded GPS slots and a 48-hour jail cap for technical violations, my only leverage with high-risk noncompliance is a warning they know I can’t back up.

This person is a 38-year-old formerly incarcerated mother in Houston who works a retail job and urges decarceration paired with reentry infrastructure: guaranteed transitional housing vouchers, immediate state IDs and Medicaid activation pre-release, Pell-funded prison education, childcare support, and automatic record sealing after a crime-free period, because she struggled to regain custody and employment despite completing treatment and vocational programs. In Harris County I waited eight weeks for my state ID after release, which cost me a job offer and a lease, so same-day IDs at the gate are my top priority. I favor automatic record sealing after three clean years because I couldn't afford the $600 in fees to file a petition. A six-month reentry housing voucher would have let me reunify with my kids sooner, since the shelter I stayed in didn’t allow children and every landlord refused to rent to me without an ID. Right now my background check keeps me capped at 29 hours at the store, so automatic, fee-free sealing after three clean years would finally let me move to full-time with benefits.

This person is a 67-year-old neighborhood association president in Boston, a retired teacher, who supports fewer people in prison but wants implementation to include zoning and siting standards for reentry housing (caps per block, 24/7 onsite staff), community benefit agreements, data sharing on outcomes, and rapid-response nuisance abatement, citing past experiences with poorly managed halfway houses concentrating impacts on one street. Back in 2001, a cluster of three halfway houses opened on my block and I ended up logging nightly incidents for the precinct, which is why I now insist on enforceable per-block caps and 48-hour nuisance abatement triggers. In 2015 our association negotiated a community benefit agreement with a sober home that funded a part-time outreach worker and cut 911 calls on our block by half, which is why I insist on enforceable CBAs and 24/7 staffing with any reentry housing. Two of my former students came home from prison and floundered without services, so I press for required case management and job placement metrics in every CBA. I live within 600 feet of a proposed reentry housing site, so I’m insisting on 24/7 staffing, a designated neighborhood liaison, and quarterly public reporting before any approval.

This person is a 29-year-old civil rights data scientist and attorney in Oakland who backs decarceration but demands safeguards: public audits of risk assessment tools, disparate impact testing, open validation studies, the right to challenge algorithmic scores, strict limits and sunset clauses on electronic monitoring, and transparent recidivism metrics, because opaque tools can entrench bias and create e-carceration instead of true population reduction. I've represented Oakland clients branded "high risk" by opaque pretrial tools and stuck in jail because there was no formal process to challenge or audit their scores. After a client spent six extra weeks in Santa Rita because a proprietary high-risk score couldn’t be challenged or audited, I’ve been pushing for a statutory right to confront and cross-examine algorithmic evidence in pretrial decisions. I watched a client’s ankle monitor flag a false “tamper” from industrial equipment at the Port of Oakland, and he was jailed for two weeks despite no new conduct. After my CPRA requests for a pretrial tool’s training data and error rates were denied as “trade secrets,” I’ve been pushing for a statutory trade‑secret carve‑out that compels disclosure when algorithms are used to restrict liberty.

This person is a 35-year-old tech product manager in Denver whose company supplies validated risk assessments and electronic monitoring, advocating that population reductions be implemented with statewide adoption of transparent, independently validated tools, open APIs for court and corrections data, pilot-to-scale pathways with outcome targets, and funding for graduated supervision, arguing these alternatives maintain safety while shrinking prison counts. After leading a Colorado pilot that cut technical violations by about 20% using transparent risk tools, I’m pushing for a statewide open-API requirement so outcomes can be audited and replicated. My younger brother's probation was revoked over a curfew app glitch, which is why I insist on transparent, auditable tools and graduated responses to technical slips. My bonus is tied to reducing revocations without increasing new offenses, so I push for outcome targets baked into contracts, not just deployment counts. If the legislature opts for proprietary black-box tools without open APIs and audit logs, my team can’t verify safety or bias and I can’t meet the outcome-based metrics my pay depends on.

This person is a 34-year-old Latina public defender in Harris County, Texas, who wants to cut pretrial detention by eliminating cash bail for low-risk charges, guaranteeing counsel at first appearance, expanding 24/7 magistrate coverage, and scaling up mental-health and LEAD diversion with transportation and housing supports; she cares because she routinely watches indigent clients sit weeks on $500 bonds for cases that later get dismissed, derailing jobs and families. I’ve spent entire weekends unable to get a magistrate while a client on a $500 trespass bond sat until Tuesday, only for the case to be dismissed. After a client lost a refinery job over a three-day weekend hold on a $500 trespass case that was dismissed, I made cutting time-to-first-appearance below 12 hours my top priority. I care most about guaranteed counsel at first appearance because without a lawyer, clients plead just to go home and end up with convictions on cases that would be dismissed. I’ve watched Spanish-speaking clients waive rights they didn’t understand because no interpreter or lawyer was present at magistration, so guaranteed counsel at first appearance is non-negotiable for me.

This person is a 52-year-old suburban county prosecutor in Maricopa County, Arizona, who supports prison reduction for low-level offenses only if diversion has clear eligibility carve-outs for repeat violent offenses, standardized risk tools, victim consultation requirements, and swift, graduated sanctions for noncompliance; he cares because failed diversions without accountability have led to new victims in his caseload and eroded public trust. After a 2018 diversion participant from his caseload assaulted a neighbor while noncompliant, he began insisting on validated risk tools and mandatory victim input before any diversion offer. He wants statutory timelines—validated risk assessment within 48 hours, documented victim contact, and violation responses within 72 hours—because weekend delays in two cases led to new assaults on his docket. He supports dedicated funding for weekend on-call risk assessors and victim advocates so the 48- and 72-hour mandates are met even over long weekends. After spending a Sunday night calling a victim’s family because a diversion violator wasn’t sanctioned until Monday, I vowed not to back any plan without funded weekend coverage and 72-hour responses.

This person is a 58-year-old rural sheriff in Boone County, West Virginia, who wants to reduce the state prison backlog by funding regional crisis-stabilization centers to avoid bookings, speeding up DOC pickups from county jails, reimbursing jail per-diem costs on time, and enabling cite-and-release for minor possession; he cares because overcrowding forces costly out-of-county transports and ties up deputies for hours. Last quarter, per diem reimbursements came 10 weeks late, forcing me to freeze overtime and delay replacing two cruisers just to keep the jail running. Last month I had to pull two deputies off the night shift to haul a detoxing inmate 90 minutes to an out-of-county jail because our beds were full, and our 911 response times doubled until they got back. If we had a 12-bed sobering and crisis unit in Madison staffed 24/7, I estimate we could avoid booking 15–20% of weekend arrests and keep at least one patrol car on the road. After visiting a neighboring county’s crisis-stabilization unit and watching them divert three intoxicated folks from jail in one Friday shift, I’m convinced we need the same model in Madison.

This person is a 46-year-old corrections officers’ union representative in Clinton County, New York, who argues decarceration must be phased with guaranteed job transfers or retraining, safe staffing ratios for higher-need remaining populations, and state-backed economic transition funds for towns when prisons close; she cares because her community’s tax base and members’ safety depend on predictable staffing and redevelopment commitments. After the last downsizing, some of my members had to choose between a demotion or 90‑minute commutes, so I want binding transfer rights within 50 miles and funded retraining. When Lyon Mountain Correctional Facility closed, my sister had to move her kids’ schools after a two-hour reassignment and our town never saw the promised redevelopment, so I now insist on enforceable transition plans with timelines. After responding to three assaults in one week on an understaffed mental health unit, I won’t back closures without mandated staffing ratios and funded de‑escalation training. Without early‑retirement options and pension‑vesting protections built into any closure plan, some of my 19‑ to 24‑year officers will miss their 25‑year retirement and lose benefits they’ve counted on.

This person is a 29-year-old Black mother in Oakland, California, formerly incarcerated on a nonviolent offense, who advocates reducing re-incarceration by capping technical parole violations, providing transitional housing vouchers, childcare-linked job training, automatic record sealing after supervision, and eliminating supervision fees; she cares because she was sent back to prison for a curfew violation and lost both housing and employment. I used to choose between paying $85 in supervision fees or buying diapers, so eliminating those fees would stop setting us up to fail. Automatic record sealing right after supervision matters most to me because two employers rescinded offers after background checks even though I’d completed every program. A BART delay made me 12 minutes past curfew and that alone sent me back, so capping technical violations would keep small slips from blowing up our lives. When my toddler had an asthma attack and I was stuck at Highland Hospital past curfew, I still got a technical violation, so there should be an emergency exemption and a warning-first policy instead of jail.

This person is a 63-year-old crime victim advocate in Minneapolis, Minnesota, who supports fewer people in prison if early releases include enforceable restitution plans, upgraded victim-notification systems, GPS monitoring for high-risk domestic violence cases, and restorative justice only with victim consent and trained facilitators; he cares because his sibling was assaulted and felt excluded from early-release decisions. He learned about his sibling’s assailant’s early release from a TV news segment instead of the state’s notice system, and the promised restitution never arrived. Because he ended up paying for his sibling’s therapy when restitution never came, he wants wage garnishment and escrowed restitution set up before any early release is approved. He now pushes for opt-out, multi-channel victim alerts with read-receipt verification after he missed the chance to object to his sibling’s assailant’s early release. Because he’s still carrying credit card debt from paying his sibling’s counseling bills, he insists restitution be escrowed and wage-garnished before any release.

This person is a 38-year-old Indian American data scientist at a Massachusetts state criminal justice agency, who favors decarceration guided by transparent, open-source risk tools with independent audits, published error rates by race/sex/age, sunset clauses if disparities persist, and public dashboards tracking outcomes of releases; he cares because he has seen opaque models produce feedback loops that undermine fair implementation. After our 2023 audit of a vendor pretrial tool found a 2x higher false-positive rate for Black women in Massachusetts, I’ve insisted on open-source code and quarterly subgroup error reports before any rollout. If the state chooses proprietary tools again, my team can’t audit subgroup errors in real time, and I’ll have to defend outcomes I can’t verify. I want the law to restrict risk scores to expanding release eligibility, never to justify detention. After I watched a judge detain a woman on a vendor score our later audit proved wrong, I became adamant that risk tools be used only to expand release.

This person is a 27-year-old Black civil rights organizer on Chicago’s South Side, who opposes proprietary risk assessments and wants legislation banning the use of arrests (without convictions) in release decisions, automatic expungement of dismissed cases, community-led restorative justice centers, and redirecting prison savings into housing and youth jobs; she cares because she has experienced over-policing and sees algorithmic bias as a new barrier. Her younger brother lost his job after spending two months in Cook County Jail on a dismissed case because a proprietary risk score labeled him “high risk.” She’s watched that dismissed arrest keep showing up on her brother’s job and housing background checks, so automatic expungement is her top priority. She volunteers at a South Side expungement clinic and sees dismissed arrests blocking jobs and apartments every week, so she insists on automatic, no-fee expungement. After her brother was evicted and lost his job during two months in Cook County Jail on a dismissed case, she insists any decarceration bill earmark savings for emergency rent relief and automatic, no-fee expungement within 30 days.

This person is a 61-year-old Cuban American drug court judge in Miami-Dade County, Florida, who seeks to reduce prison by expanding problem-solving courts, authorizing treatment in lieu of conviction, guaranteeing immediate MAT access (methadone/buprenorphine), funding residential beds, Spanish-language counseling, transportation vouchers, and automatic expungement upon completion; he cares because timely treatment dramatically lowers reoffending in his court. Without guaranteed same-day MAT in the jail, I've watched otherwise eligible participants relapse during intake delays and come back on new charges. Automatic expungement upon completion is the linchpin in Miami, because my graduates keep losing port and hospitality jobs over old possession cases unless we clear their records. I’ve written dozens of letters to PortMiami and hotel HR to vouch for graduates, which is why expungement must be automatic and fee-free rather than a petition process most can’t navigate. I’m pushing for pre-plea diversion with dismissal instead of post-plea “withholds,” because those still block TWIC cards and port badges my graduates need to work at PortMiami.

This person is a 49-year-old Korean American probation supervisor in Los Angeles County, California, who supports decarceration only with funding to cap caseloads around 40:1, implement a violation-response matrix with incentives, deploy CBT programs, replace fees with service supports, and upgrade integrated case management IT; she cares because overloaded supervision without resources leads to avoidable revocations back to prison. In a six-month pilot with 40:1 caps and an incentives-based violation matrix, my unit cut technical revocations by about 30%, so I’m pushing to scale it countywide. I still remember having to violate a young father after two missed check-ins because he couldn’t afford supervision fees or a bus pass, which is why I’m adamant about replacing fees with service supports and an integrated case management system. If decarceration moves ahead without funding those pieces, my officers’ caseloads will jump back over 80:1 and I’ll be signing more violation packets that undo the whole point. My officers currently lose nearly two hours a day double-entering notes across three legacy systems, so an integrated case management platform is the difference between coaching clients and pushing paperwork.

This person is a state prison warden in Ohio, age 54, who supports reducing the population by expanding geriatric parole eligibility to 55+, revising earned-time credits up to 20% for evidence-based vocational and cognitive behavioral programs, and sequencing facility downsizing with staff redeployment plans; they care because an aging incarcerated population has doubled medical costs and contributed to violence, and their pilot step-down unit cut serious incidents by 18% in a year. I’ve had to lock down two housing units to cover ER escorts for men in wheelchairs, which is exactly the kind of avoidable strain these reforms would relieve. I care most about pairing 55+ geriatric parole with funded staff redeployment, so I don’t lose veteran officers to county jobs as beds close. When we mothballed a dorm last spring without redeployment funds, I lost three veteran COs to county jobs, so 55+ parole must be paired with guaranteed retraining and placement timelines. If earned-time is raised to 20% without funding enough CBT and vocational seats, I’ll have hundreds eligible on paper with nowhere to earn credits, driving grievances and yard tension.

This person is a corrections officers’ union representative in rural Ohio, age 42, who will only back population reductions if the state enacts binding minimum staffing ratios, funds paid retraining pipelines into probation and behavioral health roles, guarantees no involuntary layoffs for three years, and offers hazard pay during transitions; they care because sudden unit closures have previously left members short-staffed and unsafe while local economies depend on these jobs. When the state mothballed a dorm at our facility in 2021, I pulled back-to-back 16s for weeks and watched assaults jump because critical posts went uncovered. What matters most to me is state-funded, paid retraining slots into probation and behavioral health right here in our region, so my members aren’t forced to uproot their families for jobs two counties over. I want the bill to fund paid retraining seats at our local community college with guaranteed placement into our county probation and behavioral health openings. We lost three seasoned officers to jobs two counties over last year because there wasn’t a funded local pathway into probation, and I won’t support any plan that repeats that.

This person is a public defender in Phoenix, age 33, who pushes for decarceration by eliminating cash bail for misdemeanors, adopting validated risk-based release with next-court-date text reminders, creating weekend arraignments to avoid 72-hour jail holds, and expanding pretrial services; they care because clients routinely lose jobs and housing after short jail stays, and court appearance rates in their pilot rose with reminders and transportation vouchers. I still think about a client jailed from Friday to Monday on a $250 misdemeanor bond who was fired by Tuesday—exactly why I’m fighting hardest for countywide weekend arraignments. If we swap cash bail for ankle monitors and strict check-ins without funding reminders and transit, I’ll just watch my clients rack up technical violations and lose the same jobs we’re trying to protect. I keep a stack of Valley Metro passes at my desk because a $4 bus fare is often the difference between making court and getting a bench warrant for my clients. In our office’s pilot, bilingual text reminders and Valley Metro passes cut failures to appear by about 30%, so getting those funded countywide is my nonnegotiable.

This person is a county prosecutor in Maricopa County, age 50, who accepts targeted decarceration only if repeat violent offenses are excluded, victims are consulted before diversion, and risk tools are independently audited for racial bias with transparent release criteria; they care because case outcomes and community safety depend on credible constraints and because past unaudited tools produced inconsistent results. After an unaudited risk score in one of my cases greenlit release and the defendant committed an aggravated assault, I won’t support any decarceration plan without independent audits and clear release criteria. I’m the one who must explain releases to victims and judges, so I need public, audited false‑negative rates by offense type and clear override rules before supporting diversion. After too many 11 p.m. first‑appearance dockets where releases swung by judge and shift, I need audited tools and posted criteria so I can defend decisions to victims and the court. If we expand diversion without audited false‑negative thresholds by offense and a public override log, my plea leverage and victim cooperation will erode when releases look arbitrary.

This person is a formerly incarcerated father and small-business owner in Detroit, age 39, who advocates for automatic record sealing after three conviction-free years, state-funded transitional housing vouchers on release, guaranteed state ID and licensing help at the gate, and performance-based grants to employers who hire returnees; they care because a stale felony record and lack of housing blocked contracts despite full compliance and training. I lost a $50,000 city snow-removal contract and a shop lease because my decade-old felony wasn’t sealed, even after three conviction-free years. I care most about automatic record sealing at three conviction-free years, because the petition process cost me $1,200 and six months that cost me jobs. Automatic should mean no petition, no fees, and seals pushed to private background-check databases within 30 days, because bid windows are short and every delay costs me contracts. I’ve had two trained drivers sent back to prison over missed check-ins, blowing deadlines and contracts, which is why I want fewer technical lockups and faster automatic record sealing.

This person is a suburban homeowner and taxpayer in Oakland County, Michigan, age 67 and on a fixed income, who supports decarceration only if a statutory budget lockbox dedicates documented savings to property tax relief, local victim services, and neighborhood patrols, with quarterly public dashboards on recidivism and costs and a five-year sunset requiring reauthorization; they care about fiscal accountability and visible community benefits. After her car was stolen from her driveway in Rochester Hills last summer, she’ll only support decarceration if verified savings show up as a line on her property tax bill and fund extra neighborhood patrols and victim services. After paying a $500 insurance deductible and replacing her house locks when the thief took her spare key, she wants savings earmarked for victim reimbursements like deductibles and locksmith fees. Since her car was never recovered and no one was charged, she wants an audited county fund that reimburses deductibles and locksmith costs within 30 days, itemized as a credit on her property tax bill. She wants a hard trigger that pauses any decarceration plan if auto thefts or recidivism rise in her ZIP code for two consecutive quarters.

This person is a rural county commissioner in Mingo County, West Virginia, age 61, whose county budget relies on per-diem jail contracts; they oppose rapid reductions unless the state creates a transition fund, repurposes the jail into a treatment and workforce training center with guaranteed broadband and capital grants, and backfills lost revenue for five years; they care because prior state policy changes hollowed out local revenues and jobs. I’m still paying off a 20-year bond on our 2016 jail expansion that we justified with state per-diem contracts, so sudden reductions would blow a hole in our budget. When coal severance tanked, I had to lay off deputies and close a satellite 911 station, so I won’t back inmate reductions without a guaranteed five-year backfill and funds to repurpose the jail with broadband. Our jail bond covenants require at least a 1.2x debt-service coverage, and a 20% drop in per-diem inmate days would put us in technical default and spike our interest costs. I’ve already scoped converting two housing pods into a 40-bed medication-assisted treatment unit and a welding/lineman training lab, but it only pencils out if the state puts up roughly $3 million in capital and guarantees fiber to the building.

This person is an urban emergency department director in Baltimore, age 45, who supports reducing incarceration by scaling 24/7 crisis stabilization centers, integrating 988 with police drop-off protocols guaranteeing a 30-minute transfer, suspending—not terminating—Medicaid during incarceration with automatic reinstatement at release, and funding medication-assisted treatment behind the walls; they care because ED boarding of people in crisis leads to arrests that clinical care could prevent. Last winter I watched a man in opioid withdrawal wait 17 hours in our hallway only to be arrested for disorderly conduct—an outcome a timely crisis bed could have prevented. Without an enforceable 30-minute 988/police drop-off handoff to a crisis center, officers keep defaulting to my ED or central booking, and the de-escalation window closes fast. If Medicaid is terminated during incarceration, my team loses precious hours re-enrolling people at release while they miss meds and spiral back into our ED or central booking. As the person accountable for ED throughput and staff safety, every missed 30-minute 988 handoff becomes an all-night board that forces ambulance diversion and steers officers back to central booking.

This person is a restorative justice facilitator and survivor of a home burglary in Portland, age 36, who supports decarceration conditioned on victim-centered alternatives: pre-charge conferences, restitution plans enforced by community accountability boards, state-funded trauma therapy, and compliance tracking with measurable milestones; they care because their case resolved without incarceration, delivered restitution, and reduced their fear of reoffense. They worry that decarceration without dedicated therapy funding and enforceable, time-bound restitution would shift both costs and risk back onto victims like them. In my case, I only got my locks and laptop replaced because the community accountability board enforced a six-month restitution schedule and verified each payment. I care most about restitution being enforceable—automatic wage garnishment and a state victims’ fund that fronts payments when milestones are missed—so costs don’t fall back on victims. When the third payment in my case was missed, the board triggered wage garnishment and I finally got paid within two pay cycles.

This person is a survivor of an aggravated assault in Houston, age 58, who opposes sentence reductions for violent and gun offenses and wants any decarceration plan to exclude those categories, mandate GPS monitoring and strict no-contact orders for early releases, and require immediate custody if conditions are violated; they care because the assailant’s early release in a prior case led to intimidation and ongoing safety concerns. After his early release, he twice sat in a car outside my house despite a no-contact order, and police said they couldn’t detain him unless he stepped onto my property. I want GPS exclusion zones with real-time victim alerts so that if he comes within two blocks of my home, police must take him into custody. After the second time, I stayed at my sister’s for two weeks and missed work, which is why I insist on GPS exclusion zones that trigger immediate custody if breached. I installed security cameras and filed two police reports with timestamps and plate photos, yet it still wasn’t enough to detain him under the current no-contact rules.
